plan.contextChunk: This figure places two oblique triangles side by side in plain black outline, lettered identically, to contrast where the altitude lands. In each one the horizontal base is labeled b and runs from the vertex alpha at the left to the vertex gamma at the right, the apex is labeled beta, the short left side from alpha to beta is labeled c, and the long side sloping from beta down to gamma is labeled a. In the left triangle the apex sits above the interior of the base, and a dashed vertical altitude labeled h drops from beta to a point on b, meeting it at a small square marking the right angle; an arc at alpha marks the interior angle. In the right triangle the apex has shifted left beyond alpha, making the angle there obtuse, so the dashed altitude falls outside the figure and the base is carried leftward by a dashed extension to receive its foot. Two arcs appear at that lower left corner, one for the interior angle alpha and, immediately left of it, one for the angle alpha prime between side c and the extension. Setting the arrangements against each other shows that the same height construction serves both, provided the angle used is the one adjacent to the perpendicular, which supplies h for computing the area of a triangle with no right angle of its own.

interactionPlan.concept: The area of any oblique triangle equals one-half the base times the perpendicular height from the opposite vertex, and that height is the leg of a right triangle giving h = c·sin of the angle adjacent to the perpendicular — whether the foot lands on the base (acute) or on its extension (obtuse).

interactions.label: Apex β horizontal position
interactions.teaches: Dragging β horizontally across α slides the altitude foot from inside the base onto the dashed extension, and the angle that supplies the height switches from the interior α to its supplement α′ — the perpendicular construction itself never changes, only where it lands.

interactions.label: Angle at α
interactions.teaches: The two named cases differ only in whether the perpendicular from β meets the segment b or its extension; in both, h = c·sin of the angle adjacent to the perpendicular, so the same area formula applies.

interactions.label: Construct altitude h (click base b)
interactions.teaches: Dropping the perpendicular converts the oblique triangle into a right triangle whose vertical leg h is exactly the height used in Area = ½·b·h, linking the slanted side c and the angle to the area via h = c·sin α.

demo_steps.title: An oblique triangle
demo_steps.narration: Base b runs from α to γ with apex β above; sides a and c carry no right angle, so the usual ½·base·height needs a height we must construct.

demo_steps.title: Drop the perpendicular
demo_steps.narration: Clicking the base drops the dashed altitude h from β with a right-angle marker; h is the leg opposite α in a right triangle with hypotenuse c, so h = c·sin α and Area = ½·b·c·sin α.

demo_steps.title: Obtuse arrangement
demo_steps.narration: Snapping to the obtuse case moves β left of α; the altitude foot now falls outside the triangle on the dashed base extension, and the relevant angle is the exterior α′ = 180° − α, yet sin α′ = sin α so the formula is unchanged.

demo_steps.title: Sweep the apex
demo_steps.narration: Drag β continuously across α and watch the foot slide from the interior of b onto the extension while the labeled angle flips from α to α′ — one height construction serves every oblique triangle.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Whether the perpendicular from the apex lands on the base or on its extension, the height is h = c·sin of the angle adjacent to that perpendicular, so Area = ½·b·c·sin α holds for acute and obtuse triangles alike.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Render a single morphing oblique triangle on a horizontal base b (α left, γ right) rather than two static panels; the toggle simply snaps the apex to a representative acute (β right of α) or obtuse (β left of α) position. Triangle outline solid black; altitude h and the base extension dashed gray; angle arcs in red with α (and α′ in the obtuse case) labeled in italic serif; right-angle foot shown as a small open square. The α′ arc and the dashed leftward extension appear only when β is left of α (obtuse), driven by the apex position so they stay correct even after free dragging. Reveal the 'Area = ½·b·c·sin α' annotation together with the altitude. Keep vertex and side labels (α, β, γ, a, b, c) fixed relative to their edges as the apex moves.

authoredContext:
Now that we can solve a triangle for missing values, we can use some of those values and the sine function to find the area of an oblique triangle. Recall that the area formula for a triangle is given as Area= 1 2 bh, where b is base and h is height. For oblique triangles, we must find h before we can use the area formula. Observing the two triangles in the figure, one acute and one obtuse, we can drop a perpendicular to represent the height and then apply the trigonometric property sinα= opposite hypotenuse to write an equation for area in oblique triangles. In the acute triangle, we have sinα= h c or csinα=h. However, in the obtuse triangle, we drop the perpendicular outside the triangle and extend the base b to form a right triangle. The angle used in calculation is α ′, or 180−α.

Two oblique triangles with standard labels. Both have a dotted altitude line h extended from angle beta to the horizontal base side b. In the first, which is an acute triangle, the altitude is within the triangle. In the second, which is an obtuse triangle, the altitude h is outside of the triangle.
